title: Module 1: Bioenergetics and ATP
mission: Build a working map of metabolism, free energy, enzyme kinetics, and ATP so you can predict reaction direction and recognize how cells couple energy.
primer: Metabolism is the complete set of enzyme-catalyzed chemical reactions in a cell; catabolism breaks molecules down and releases usable energy, while anabolism uses energy to build cellular molecules.

Catabolic pathways usually converge from many nutrients toward fewer common products, while anabolic pathways usually diverge from a few precursors toward many products; separate enzymes help prevent wasteful cycling.
For an enzyme following Michaelis-Menten behavior, Vmax is the rate reached at saturating substrate, and Km is the substrate concentration at which the rate equals half of Vmax.
Free-energy change combines bonding stability and disorder: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS. A negative ΔG favors the forward direction, a positive ΔG favors the reverse direction, and ΔG = 0 means equilibrium.
The biochemical standard state uses pH 7 and treats water as 55.5 M. The transformed standard free-energy change is written ΔG°′ and relates to equilibrium by ΔG°′ = -RT ln K′eq.

Actual cellular reaction direction depends on both the standard value and concentrations: ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln([products]/[reactants]). ΔG values add when reactions are coupled through shared intermediates.
ATP hydrolysis has ΔG°′ about -30.5 kJ/mol, but its actual ΔG in a cell differs because ATP, ADP, phosphate, and Mg2+ concentrations are not at standard conditions.

ATP often powers work by transferring a phosphoryl or adenylyl group and changing a substrate or protein, rather than by releasing energy through isolated hydrolysis; examples include molecular motion, DNA-associated enzymes, and firefly light production.

recall.q: What is the difference between catabolism and anabolism?
recall.a: Catabolism degrades molecules and releases usable energy; anabolism consumes energy to synthesize cellular molecules.

recall.q: Why do cells commonly use separate enzymes for opposing anabolic and catabolic pathways?
recall.a: Separate control prevents both directions from running strongly at once and wasting energy in a futile cycle.

recall.q: What do Vmax and Km mean in Michaelis-Menten kinetics?
recall.a: Vmax is the maximum rate at saturating substrate, and Km is the substrate concentration at which the rate is half of Vmax.

recall.q: What does the sign of ΔG tell you?
recall.a: Negative ΔG favors the forward reaction, positive ΔG favors the reverse reaction, and zero ΔG indicates equilibrium.

recall.q: How are ΔG°′ and the equilibrium constant related?
recall.a: ΔG°′ = -RT ln K′eq; a larger equilibrium constant therefore corresponds to a more negative ΔG°′.

recall.q: Why can the actual ΔG of a reaction differ from ΔG°′?
recall.a: Actual ΔG also depends on the current concentrations of products and reactants through RT ln([products]/[reactants]).

recall.q: What happens to free-energy changes when reactions are coupled?
recall.a: Their ΔG values add, so a sufficiently favorable reaction can make the overall coupled process favorable.

recall.q: What is the true ATP-containing substrate for many ATP-dependent enzymes in the cytosol?
recall.a: MgATP2+, because Mg2+ binds ATP and participates in the form recognized by many enzymes.

mcqs.q: Which statement best describes the usual organization of metabolic pathways?
options: Catabolic pathways diverge and anabolic pathways converge
Both catabolic and anabolic pathways are always linear
Catabolic pathways converge and anabolic pathways diverge
The same enzyme must catalyze both directions of every pathway
mcqs.explanation: Many nutrients feed into fewer catabolic products, while a smaller set of precursors supplies many anabolic products.

mcqs.q: An enzyme-catalyzed reaction is running at half of Vmax. For a simple Michaelis-Menten enzyme, the substrate concentration equals:
mcqs.explanation: Km is defined numerically as the substrate concentration at which velocity is half of Vmax.

mcqs.q: A reaction has a large negative ΔG under the current cellular conditions. What is the best conclusion?
mcqs.explanation: A negative actual ΔG supplies a thermodynamic driving force toward products.

mcqs.q: Which condition defines equilibrium for a reaction?
mcqs.explanation: At equilibrium there is no net driving force, so the actual free-energy change is zero.

mcqs.q: Which expression includes the effect of cellular reactant and product concentrations?
mcqs.explanation: The reaction quotient term adjusts the standard free energy for the concentrations that actually exist.

mcqs.q: Reaction A has ΔG = +10 kJ/mol and a coupled reaction B has ΔG = -25 kJ/mol. What is the overall ΔG?
mcqs.explanation: Free-energy changes are additive: +10 + (-25) = -15 kJ/mol, so the coupled process is favorable.

mcqs.q: Why is the actual free energy of ATP hydrolysis in a living cell not necessarily -30.5 kJ/mol?
options: ATP cannot be hydrolyzed inside cells
Cellular ATP, ADP, and Pi concentrations differ from standard-state concentrations
Enzymes reverse the sign of ΔG
ATP hydrolysis does not involve water
mcqs.explanation: The quoted value is a transformed standard value; actual ΔG depends on cellular concentrations and Mg2+ binding.

mcqs.q: Which example best matches the slides' statement that ATP provides energy by group transfer?
options: ATP remains unchanged while heating the cytosol
ATP transfers a group that drives a protein through different conformations
ATP removes all enzymes from a pathway
ATP changes ΔG°′ by changing temperature
mcqs.explanation: Transferred groups can create activated intermediates or alter protein conformation, coupling ATP use to chemical or mechanical work.

traps: Do not treat ΔG°′ as the same as actual ΔG; only actual ΔG includes the current concentration ratio.
A favorable negative ΔG predicts direction, not speed; an enzyme changes rate but does not change the reaction's ΔG.
Km is a substrate concentration at half Vmax, not the maximum rate itself.
ATP does not merely release free energy as heat; useful coupling commonly involves group transfer and MgATP2+.
checkpoint: Without notes, write the three ΔG cases and the direction each predicts.
Explain in two sentences how a +ΔG reaction can proceed when coupled to ATP use.
Sketch a Michaelis-Menten curve and label Vmax, half Vmax, and Km.

title: Module 2: Gene Expression and the Lac Operon
sourcePages: Gene Expression and Regulation ppt.pptx, slides 1-35
mission: Follow information from DNA to protein and use lactose and glucose levels to predict lac-operon transcription.
primer: The central dogma describes residue-by-residue information flow from DNA to RNA to protein. Replication copies DNA, transcription makes RNA from DNA, and translation uses mRNA to make protein.
DNA replication occurs during S phase and is semiconservative, so each daughter DNA molecule contains one parental strand and one newly synthesized strand.
RNA polymerase binds a promoter, opens a transcription bubble, escapes the promoter, elongates the RNA, and terminates transcription. It reads the template or antisense strand.

The coding or sense DNA strand matches the mRNA sequence except that DNA has thymine where RNA has uracil. Eukaryotic pre-mRNA contains exons and introns, and splicing removes introns to produce mature mRNA.
Translation occurs on ribosomes in the cytoplasm. The ribosome reads mRNA 5′ to 3′, tRNAs deliver amino acids, and the protein grows from its N terminus toward its C terminus.

Prokaryotes regulate gene expression mainly at transcription initiation, and transcription can occur alongside translation because there is no nucleus. Eukaryotes can regulate transcription, RNA processing, RNA transport, and translation.

An operon is a prokaryotic cluster of genes transcribed from one promoter as a single mRNA. In the lac operon, lacZ encodes β-galactosidase, lacY encodes lactose permease, and lacA encodes transacetylase.

Strong lac-operon transcription requires lactose present and glucose absent: allolactose removes the repressor from the operator, while low glucose raises cAMP, activates CAP, and helps RNA polymerase bind.

recall.q: State the central dogma in one line.
recall.a: Genetic information normally flows from DNA to RNA to protein.

recall.q: What does semiconservative DNA replication produce?
recall.a: Each daughter DNA molecule contains one old parental strand and one newly synthesized strand.

recall.q: Which DNA strand serves as the template for mRNA, and how does the other strand compare with mRNA?
recall.a: RNA polymerase reads the template or antisense strand; the coding or sense strand has the mRNA sequence except T replaces U.

recall.q: What processing converts eukaryotic pre-mRNA into mature mRNA in these slides?
recall.a: Splicing removes noncoding introns and joins the coding exons.

recall.q: In which directions are mRNA read and protein synthesized?
recall.a: mRNA is read 5′ to 3′, and protein is synthesized from the N terminus to the C terminus.

recall.q: What is an operon?
recall.a: A cluster of prokaryotic genes controlled by one promoter and transcribed together as a single mRNA.

recall.q: What are the distinct jobs of the lac repressor and CAP?
recall.a: The repressor blocks transcription at the operator when lactose is absent; active CAP promotes RNA polymerase binding when glucose is low.

recall.q: What exact nutrient condition gives strong lac-operon transcription?
recall.a: Lactose must be present and glucose must be absent.

mcqs.q: Which product is made directly by transcription?
mcqs.explanation: RNA polymerase uses a DNA template to synthesize RNA.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the coding DNA strand is correct?
options: It is identical to mRNA, including uracil
It is complementary to mRNA at every base
It matches mRNA except that it contains thymine instead of uracil
It is removed during RNA splicing
mcqs.explanation: The coding strand and mRNA carry the same base sequence when T in DNA is treated as U in RNA.

mcqs.q: A newly made eukaryotic pre-mRNA contains:
mcqs.explanation: Splicing removes introns from an exon-plus-intron precursor to form mature mRNA.

mcqs.q: During translation, which pairing of directions is correct?
options: mRNA 3′ to 5′; protein C terminus to N terminus
mRNA 5′ to 3′; protein N terminus to C terminus
mRNA 5′ to 3′; protein C terminus to N terminus
mRNA direction varies; protein always begins at the C terminus
mcqs.explanation: The ribosome moves along mRNA 5′ to 3′ and adds residues to the C end of a chain that began at its N terminus.

mcqs.q: Why can transcription and translation occur at the same time in prokaryotes?
options: Prokaryotes lack compartmentalization by a nucleus
mcqs.explanation: Without a nuclear barrier, ribosomes can begin translating an mRNA while RNA polymerase is still transcribing it.

mcqs.q: Which lac-operon component is correctly matched with its product?
mcqs.explanation: The slide assigns lacZ to β-galactosidase, lacY to permease, and lacA to transacetylase.

mcqs.q: Lactose is present and glucose is also present. What level of lac-operon transcription is expected?
options: Strong transcription because CAP is active
Low, leaky transcription because the repressor is released but CAP is inactive
No transcription because allolactose strengthens repressor binding
Strong transcription because cAMP is high
mcqs.explanation: Allolactose removes the repressor, but high glucose keeps cAMP low and CAP inactive, so transcription remains low.

mcqs.q: Glucose is absent, but lactose is also absent. What prevents lac-operon transcription?
options: The lac repressor remains bound to the operator
mcqs.explanation: Low glucose activates CAP, but without lactose there is no allolactose to remove the repressor, which remains a roadblock.

traps: Replication copies DNA; transcription makes RNA; translation makes protein. Similar wording in options often hides a process swap.
The template strand is the antisense strand; the coding strand resembles mRNA except for T versus U.
Lactose removes negative control, but strong expression also needs low glucose to activate CAP through cAMP.
CAP is a positive regulator and the lac repressor is a negative regulator; both act at different DNA sites.
checkpoint: Close the slides and draw DNA to RNA to protein, adding location, enzyme or machine, and direction.
Make a four-row lactose/glucose table and predict none, low, or strong transcription.
Recite lacZ, lacY, and lacA with one function each.

title: Module 3: Genetic Engineering Toolkit
mission: Trace a gene from isolation to a verified recombinant clone and identify the tool responsible for each step.
primer: Genetic engineering deliberately modifies genetic material by isolating, changing, and transferring DNA. A gene of interest can be placed in a vector, introduced into a host, replicated, and sometimes expressed as a product.

The core cloning workflow is gene isolation or PCR, cutting insert and vector with compatible restriction enzymes, ligation, transfer into a host, selection and screening, then expression or other downstream use.
Restriction endonucleases recognize specific short DNA sequences, often palindromic, and cut DNA to create sticky or blunt ends. Using the same enzyme on vector and insert can create compatible ends.

DNA ligase seals the sugar-phosphate backbone by forming a phosphodiester bond between a 3′-OH and a 5′-phosphate. T4 DNA ligase uses ATP, and sticky ends usually ligate more efficiently than blunt ends.
PCR amplifies a chosen DNA region through repeated denaturation, primer annealing, and extension. Ideal amplification after n cycles is approximately 2^n copies.
Agarose gel electrophoresis separates negatively charged DNA by size. DNA moves toward the positive electrode, and smaller fragments travel faster and farther through the gel.
Sanger sequencing mixes normal dNTPs with chain-terminating ddNTPs. A ddNTP lacks a 3′-OH, so its incorporation stops synthesis and produces fragments that reveal the sequence.

CRISPR-Cas9 uses a guide RNA to direct Cas9 to a target sequence and make a double-strand break. A useful vector typically contains an origin of replication, selectable marker, and cloning site, with expression elements added when protein production is required.

recall.q: Put the six basic genetic-engineering stages in order.
recall.a: Isolate or amplify the gene, cut gene and vector, ligate them, introduce the recombinant vector into a host, select and screen clones, then express or use the verified construct.

recall.q: What is the difference between a vector and a host cell?
recall.a: A vector is the DNA carrier for the foreign sequence; the host cell receives and maintains or expresses that recombinant DNA.

recall.q: Why are the same restriction enzymes often used on the insert and vector?
recall.a: They generate compatible DNA ends that can base-pair and be joined by ligase.

recall.q: What chemical bond does DNA ligase form, and between which groups?
recall.a: It forms a phosphodiester bond between an adjacent 3′-OH and 5′-phosphate.

recall.q: Name the three repeating PCR steps in order.
recall.a: Denaturation, annealing, and extension.

recall.q: Why do smaller DNA fragments move farther in an agarose gel?
recall.a: The gel acts as a molecular sieve, so smaller fragments pass through its pores more easily.

recall.q: Why does incorporation of a ddNTP terminate Sanger DNA synthesis?
recall.a: A ddNTP lacks the 3′-OH needed to form the next phosphodiester bond.

recall.q: What are three general features expected in a useful cloning vector?
recall.a: An origin of replication, a selectable marker, and a site for insertion such as a multiple cloning site.

mcqs.q: Which sequence gives the correct basic order for making recombinant DNA in a host?
options: Ligate, isolate gene, cut DNA, select host
Isolate gene, cut insert and vector, ligate, introduce into host
Introduce into host, cut vector, amplify gene, ligate
Select clones, remove vector, isolate gene, translate
mcqs.explanation: The insert must first be obtained, compatible DNA ends created, and recombinant DNA assembled before host introduction.

mcqs.q: What is the main role of a selectable marker in a vector?
options: Cut the vector at a palindrome
Identify cells that contain the vector under selective conditions
mcqs.explanation: A selectable marker, often an antibiotic-resistance gene, allows vector-containing cells to survive or otherwise be selected.

mcqs.q: A restriction enzyme is most accurately described as an enzyme that:
options: Recognizes a specific DNA sequence and cuts at or near it
mcqs.explanation: Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at defined recognition sequences, many of which are palindromic.

mcqs.q: Why is sticky-end ligation generally more efficient than blunt-end ligation?
options: Complementary overhangs base-pair and hold fragments together
Blunt ends lack phosphate groups in every case
Sticky ends do not require DNA ligase
mcqs.explanation: Base pairing between complementary overhangs aligns the fragments and raises their effective local concentration; ligase is still required.

mcqs.q: Which event occurs during the annealing step of PCR?
mcqs.explanation: After heat separates the strands, cooling allows primers to hybridize to their complementary sites.

mcqs.q: A DNA sample is placed in an agarose gel. In which direction does it migrate, and which fragments travel farther?
options: Toward the negative electrode; larger fragments
Toward the positive electrode; smaller fragments
Toward the positive electrode; larger fragments
Toward the wells; all fragments equally
mcqs.explanation: DNA has a negatively charged phosphate backbone, and smaller fragments move more easily through the agarose network.

mcqs.q: Which property makes a ddNTP a chain terminator in Sanger sequencing?
options: It contains an extra phosphate backbone
mcqs.explanation: Without a 3′-OH, the growing strand cannot form the next phosphodiester bond.

mcqs.q: In CRISPR-Cas9 editing, what gives the system its target specificity?
options: A guide RNA complementary to the target DNA
mcqs.explanation: The guide RNA directs Cas9 to the matching DNA sequence, where Cas9 introduces a double-strand break.

traps: Restriction enzymes cut DNA; DNA ligase joins DNA. Questions often swap these two roles.
Selection finds cells carrying the vector, while screening verifies which selected clones contain the desired insert.
DNA moves toward the positive electrode because its phosphate backbone is negative; smaller fragments migrate farther.
PCR amplifies DNA, Sanger sequencing reads DNA, and CRISPR-Cas9 edits a targeted DNA site.
checkpoint: On blank paper, draw the cloning workflow and write one tool beside every step.
Explain sticky ends versus blunt ends and why one usually ligates more efficiently.
Compare PCR, gel electrophoresis, Sanger sequencing, and CRISPR-Cas9 in one sentence each.
